questions.question: What is Amazon SNS and what problem does it solve?
questions.answer: Amazon SNS (Simple Notification Service) is a fully managed publish-subscribe messaging service. It solves the problem of reliably delivering notifications and messages to multiple recipients simultaneously. Without SNS, you'd need to maintain your own notification infrastructure — email servers, SMS gateways, and subscriber management. SNS handles all of this at scale, allowing publishers (applications, AWS services, or users) to send a single message that fans out to all subscribers instantly.

questions.question: Explain the difference between a Publisher and a Subscriber in SNS.
questions.answer: A Publisher is any entity that sends a message to an SNS Topic — it could be a developer publishing manually through the console, an application sending alerts, or an AWS service like CloudWatch or Auto Scaling sending event notifications. A Subscriber is an endpoint that has opted in to receive messages from a topic — examples include email addresses, phone numbers (SMS), SQS queues, Lambda functions, and HTTP endpoints. The Topic acts as the intermediary: it receives from publishers and delivers to all subscribers.

questions.question: What is the difference between SNS Standard and FIFO topics?
questions.answer: SNS Standard topics support all subscription protocols (email, SMS, SQS, Lambda, HTTP/S, mobile push) and deliver messages with best-effort ordering — messages generally arrive in order but it's not guaranteed. SNS FIFO topics strictly preserve message order and eliminate duplicates, but they ONLY support SQS FIFO queues as subscribers. Use Standard when you need broad delivery across many protocol types. Use FIFO when strict message ordering is a business requirement, such as financial transactions or order processing.

questions.question: What is Amazon CloudWatch and what are its core components?
questions.answer: Amazon CloudWatch is AWS's monitoring and observability service. Its core components are: Metrics (numerical time-series measurements like CPU utilization, request count), Logs (text records stored in Log Groups — application output, system events, Lambda execution), Alarms (rules that watch metrics and trigger actions when thresholds are breached), and Dashboards (customizable views showing multiple metrics in one screen). Together these give you complete visibility into your AWS resources and applications.

questions.question: What are the three states of a CloudWatch Alarm?
questions.answer: A CloudWatch Alarm has three states: OK (the metric is within the defined threshold — everything is normal), In Alarm (the metric has crossed the threshold — the alarm triggers configured actions like SNS notification or EC2 stop), and Insufficient Data (the alarm was just created or there isn't enough metric data yet to determine the state). A newly created alarm always starts in Insufficient Data and transitions to OK once it has enough data points to evaluate.

questions.question: What is AWS Lambda and how does it differ from EC2?
questions.answer: AWS Lambda is a serverless compute service that runs code in response to events without you managing any servers. The key differences from EC2: EC2 is a virtual machine that runs 24/7 and you pay for every hour it's running regardless of whether code executes. Lambda runs only when triggered, executes for a maximum of 15 minutes, and you pay only for the milliseconds your code runs. EC2 requires you to manage the OS, patches, scaling, and infrastructure. Lambda handles all of that automatically. Use Lambda for short, event-driven tasks; use EC2 for long-running applications.

questions.question: What is the maximum timeout for a Lambda function?
questions.answer: The maximum execution timeout for a Lambda function is 15 minutes (900 seconds). The default timeout is 3 seconds. You can configure any value between 1 second and 15 minutes. If your function runs longer than the configured timeout, AWS forcibly terminates it and returns a timeout error. This 15-minute limit means Lambda is not suitable for long-running batch jobs or tasks that take hours — for those, use EC2, ECS, or AWS Batch instead.

questions.question: What is a Lambda Layer and when would you use one?
questions.answer: A Lambda Layer is a reusable ZIP archive containing dependencies, libraries, or custom runtimes that you attach to Lambda functions. You'd use a Layer when: your function depends on third-party packages (like Pillow, Pandas, or NumPy) that exceed the 50MB deployment package limit, you want to share common libraries across multiple functions without duplicating them in each deployment, or you need a custom runtime not natively supported by Lambda. Each function can have up to 5 layers attached, and layers have their own 250MB unzipped size limit.

questions.question: What are the four Golden Signals for system monitoring?
questions.answer: The four Golden Signals are: Latency — how long it takes to serve a request (e.g., API response time in milliseconds); Traffic — the demand placed on your system (e.g., requests per second); Errors — the rate of failed requests (e.g., percentage of 5xx HTTP responses); and Saturation — how 'full' your resource is (e.g., CPU at 95%, disk at 90%). Monitoring these four metrics gives a complete picture of system health and is the standard for setting up CloudWatch alarms in production environments.

questions.question: What is boto3 and what is its role in Lambda?
questions.answer: boto3 is the official AWS SDK (Software Development Kit) for Python. In Lambda, it is pre-installed in the Python runtime environment — you don't need to include it in your deployment package. It allows your Lambda function code to interact with any AWS service programmatically: creating S3 objects, stopping EC2 instances, publishing SNS messages, querying DynamoDB, and much more. Without boto3, a Python Lambda function cannot talk to other AWS services — it's the bridge between your code and the AWS APIs.

questions.question: Describe a situation where you used CloudWatch to diagnose a production issue.
questions.answer: (Situation) Our e-commerce platform's checkout API was receiving user complaints of slow response times during peak hours. (Task) I needed to identify the bottleneck within 30 minutes to minimize revenue impact. (Action) I opened the CloudWatch Dashboard, checked EC2 CPU — it was at 98% saturation. I checked the CloudWatch Alarm history and confirmed the CPU alarm had triggered 20 minutes ago, but the auto-scaling response hadn't fully kicked in. I also checked the CloudWatch Logs for the application — error rate showed database connection timeouts. (Result) The root cause was a combination of CPU saturation and database connection pool exhaustion. We scaled out the EC2 fleet and increased the DB connection limit. Response times returned to normal in 8 minutes. The monitoring data from CloudWatch was the only reason we found this so quickly.

questions.question: Walk me through how you would set up automated notifications when an S3 upload fails to process correctly.
questions.answer: (Situation) We had a data pipeline where files uploaded to S3 needed processing, and silent failures were causing data loss. (Task) Build an alerting system so the team is notified within minutes of any processing failure. (Action) I created an SNS topic called 'pipeline-failures' and subscribed the engineering team's email addresses. Then I configured the Lambda function that processes S3 uploads to publish a message to the SNS topic in its exception handler — including the filename, error message, and timestamp. I also set up a CloudWatch Alarm on the Lambda Error metric, which triggers the same SNS topic if error count exceeds 0 in any 1-minute window. (Result) We now receive two types of alerts: immediate application-level alerts from Lambda's exception handler, and metric-based backup alerts from CloudWatch. Mean time to detection dropped from hours to under 2 minutes.

questions.question: How would you implement automatic EC2 start/stop to reduce costs for a development environment?
questions.answer: (Situation) Development EC2 instances were running 24/7 but only used 9 AM–6 PM weekdays, costing the company unnecessarily. (Task) Automate start and stop to run instances only during work hours. (Action) I created two Lambda functions: one to start instances (using boto3 ec2.start_instances()) and one to stop them (ec2.stop_instances()). Both functions use boto3 to find instances tagged as Environment=Development. I then created two Amazon EventBridge rules: one cron expression for 9 AM weekdays triggering the start Lambda, and one for 6 PM weekdays triggering the stop Lambda. (Result) Development instances now run only 45 hours per week instead of 168, reducing compute costs by approximately 73%. Zero manual intervention required.

questions.question: Describe how you would architect a system to process images when they are uploaded to S3.
questions.answer: (Situation) A photo storage application needed to automatically generate thumbnails whenever users uploaded high-resolution images. (Task) Design a scalable, cost-efficient image processing pipeline. (Action) I designed an S3-triggered Lambda architecture: Users upload images to an S3 bucket's uploads/ prefix. S3 triggers a Lambda function on every PUT event. Lambda downloads the image from uploads/, uses the Pillow library (packaged as a Lambda Layer) to resize it, and saves the thumbnail to processed/. Lambda publishes a success or failure message to an SNS topic, which notifies the application backend via HTTP subscription. (Result) The pipeline processes thousands of images per day with zero server management, auto-scales to handle traffic spikes, and costs only for actual processing time — approximately 95% cheaper than running an EC2-based solution continuously.

questions.question: A Lambda function is failing silently — no errors reported, but the expected output isn't appearing. How would you debug this?
questions.answer: (Situation) A Lambda function that should rename S3 files was triggered but no renamed files appeared in the output folder. (Task) Identify the root cause of silent failure without access to a debugger. (Action) First, I checked CloudWatch Logs — navigated to /aws/lambda/[function-name] and found the latest log stream. The logs showed the function completed successfully but printed 'Source key not found' — the trigger was firing, but the event structure didn't match what the code expected. The S3 trigger was set to all object types, but the code only handled .jpg files. A .png upload was triggering the function, which then exited cleanly without doing anything. I also checked CloudWatch Metrics — Duration showed the function was running but Lambda Errors was 0, confirming no exceptions were thrown. (Result) Fixed by adding a file extension check and a log message for unsupported types. Added a CloudWatch Alarm on Lambda Duration being abnormally short as an early warning for this pattern.

questions.question: How would you handle a scenario where multiple teams need to receive different notifications from the same application event?
questions.answer: (Situation) An order placed event needed to notify the billing team, shipping team, and send an order confirmation email to the customer — each needing different information and different handling. (Task) Design a notification architecture that is decoupled and scalable. (Action) I implemented the SNS Fan-out pattern. Created one SNS topic for the 'order-placed' event. The application publishes one message to this topic per order. I added three subscriptions: an SQS queue (billing-queue) for the billing service to process asynchronously, a Lambda function for the shipping service to immediately reserve inventory, and the customer's email via the SES email subscriber. Each consumer is completely independent — failure in billing processing does not affect shipping or customer email. (Result) The architecture is fully decoupled. Adding a fourth consumer (analytics, for example) requires only a new subscription — no application code changes. This is the standard fan-out pattern for event-driven microservices.

questions.question: Explain a time when you used Lambda automation to enforce infrastructure compliance.
questions.answer: (Situation) Developers were occasionally creating EBS volumes as GP2 instead of the company-mandated GP3 standard, causing performance inconsistencies and preventing cost optimization. (Task) Automate enforcement so any GP2 volume is automatically converted to GP3. (Action) I created a Lambda function that uses boto3 to call modify_volume() and change the volume type from gp2 to gp3. For the trigger, I used Amazon EventBridge to capture CloudTrail events — specifically the CreateVolume API call. EventBridge triggers the Lambda whenever any EBS volume is created. The Lambda checks if the new volume is gp2 and converts it if so, then publishes a notification to an SNS topic alerting the team that an automatic conversion occurred. (Result) Zero GP2 volumes in production since deployment. The automation runs silently in the background and the SNS alert log gives full audit visibility.

questions.question: How do CloudWatch metrics differ from CloudWatch logs, and when do you use each?
questions.answer: (Situation) A new team member asked why we have both metrics and logs in CloudWatch, thinking they were redundant. (Task) Explain the distinction and appropriate use cases for each. (Action) I explained: Metrics are numerical time-series data points sampled periodically — CPU at 75%, 1000 requests/minute. They are great for dashboards, alarms, and trend analysis. Logs are text records of events written as they happen — application output, error messages, audit trails, Lambda print() statements. They are great for debugging, root cause analysis, and compliance. Metrics tell you what is happening (the what and how much). Logs tell you why it happened (the details and context). In practice: set CloudWatch Alarms on metrics to detect problems, then query CloudWatch Logs to diagnose the root cause. (Result) The team now uses both together: alarms for detection, logs for investigation.

questions.question: Walk me through the full flow of a CloudWatch Alarm that stops an EC2 instance when CPU exceeds 80%.
questions.answer: (Situation) Unstable EC2 instances consuming 100% CPU were crashing and causing downtime. (Task) Set up automated mitigation. (Action) Here's the full flow: (1) EC2 sends CPU Utilization metrics to CloudWatch every 5 minutes by default. (2) I created a CloudWatch Alarm watching the CPUUtilization metric for that specific instance. (3) Threshold: maximum CPU in any 1-minute period >= 80%. (4) Alarm Actions: when state changes to 'In Alarm' — send notification to SNS topic (engineering email subscribers) AND stop the EC2 instance. (5) When CPU spikes: CloudWatch detects the threshold breach, alarm state changes from OK to In Alarm, SNS sends email to the team, EC2 instance is stopped automatically. (6) Team investigates the issue, fixes the root cause, and manually restarts the instance. (Result) This pattern prevents cascading failures and forces human review before the problematic instance returns to service.

questions.question: Describe how you would monitor costs using CloudWatch and prevent bill surprises.
questions.answer: (Situation) An engineering team had a surprise $3,000 AWS bill one month after a developer accidentally left an EC2 instance running. (Task) Implement cost monitoring and alerting to prevent recurrence. (Action) First, I enabled Billing Alerts in the AWS Billing console — note this must be done in the us-east-1 (N. Virginia) region. I then created a CloudWatch Billing Alarm: metric = EstimatedCharges, currency = USD, threshold = $500. Action = SNS email notification to finance and engineering leads. I also created a secondary alarm at $200 as an early warning. Additionally, I set up AWS Budgets (separate from CloudWatch) for more granular tracking by service. (Result) The team now receives email alerts at $200 and $500 spend. We caught an accidental deployment that would have cost $800/month within 24 hours of it starting — total cost was $6.50.

questions.question: Design a serverless event processing pipeline for a retail application that must handle order creation, inventory update, and customer notification.
questions.answer: Architecture: Order Service (EC2/API Gateway) publishes an 'order-created' event to an SNS topic. Three subscribers handle parallel processing: (1) SQS queue → Inventory Lambda: Asynchronously reserves inventory items, handles failures with Dead Letter Queue (DLQ). (2) Lambda function → Notification Service: Immediately sends order confirmation email via SES and SMS via SNS to customer. (3) SQS queue → Analytics Lambda: Writes order data to DynamoDB for reporting. All Lambda functions write execution logs to CloudWatch Log Groups. CloudWatch Alarms monitor Lambda Error rate and SQS queue depth — alerts go to the ops team SNS topic. Retry logic: SQS provides built-in retry for Lambda failures. Benefits: Fully decoupled — any component can fail independently. Auto-scales with traffic. Pay-per-execution. Adding a new consumer (e.g., fraud detection) requires only adding an SNS subscription.

questions.question: How would you design a multi-region monitoring strategy using CloudWatch?
questions.answer: CloudWatch is a regional service — each region has its own metrics and dashboards. For multi-region monitoring: (1) Enable CloudWatch in each region where resources are deployed. (2) Create CloudWatch cross-account, cross-region dashboards in a central monitoring account — CloudWatch supports this natively via cross-account observability. (3) Use Amazon EventBridge (global) to collect events from all regions and route to a central SNS topic for alerting. (4) Consider CloudWatch Metric Streams to export metrics from all regions to a central data store (e.g., Amazon Kinesis Firehose → S3 → Athena). (5) For billing, always configure the billing alarm in us-east-1 as billing data is aggregated there. Trade-offs: Centralized monitoring reduces alert fragmentation but requires additional IAM cross-account permissions and potentially higher data transfer costs.

questions.question: Explain the event-driven architecture pattern and how SNS, Lambda, and S3 work together in it.
questions.answer: Event-driven architecture (EDA) is a design pattern where services communicate through events rather than direct API calls. Components react to events asynchronously, enabling loose coupling. Example with SNS + Lambda + S3: User uploads a photo to S3 (upload event). S3 sends a PUT notification to SNS topic 'new-uploads'. SNS fans out to two Lambda functions: Thumbnail-Lambda (resizes image, saves to processed-images/ S3 bucket) and Metadata-Lambda (extracts EXIF data, writes to DynamoDB). Each Lambda function is independent — failure in one does not affect the other. If Thumbnail-Lambda has a bug, Metadata-Lambda still runs. Benefits: Each service has a single responsibility. Scale independently. Add new consumers (virus scanner, CDN invalidation) with zero changes to existing code — just add an SNS subscription. EDA is the foundation of modern microservices on AWS.

questions.question: What are the key security considerations when configuring Lambda functions with S3 and SNS?
questions.answer: Key security considerations: (1) Principle of Least Privilege for IAM Role — the Lambda execution role should have only the specific permissions needed. Use resource-based policies: s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject on specific bucket/prefix, not s3:* on *. (2) Avoid hardcoding credentials — never put AWS access keys in Lambda code. The execution role provides automatic credential rotation. (3) Use environment variables for non-sensitive config, and AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store for sensitive values like API keys. (4) Enable Lambda function URL authentication (IAM-based) if exposing Lambda via URL — never leave it unauthenticated. (5) For SNS, use SNS Access Policy to restrict who can publish to a topic. (6) Enable VPC configuration for Lambda if it needs to access private resources (RDS in private subnet). (7) Enable CloudWatch Logs for all functions — this is your audit trail. (8) Set resource-based policies on S3 buckets to restrict Lambda access to specific functions.

questions.question: How would you handle Lambda cold start issues in a production environment?
questions.answer: A Lambda cold start occurs when AWS needs to provision a new execution environment for a function — takes 100ms to several seconds depending on runtime, package size, and VPC configuration. Impact: latency spikes on the first request after idle periods. Solutions: (1) Provisioned Concurrency — pre-warm a specified number of execution environments. They stay ready, eliminating cold starts for those requests. Cost: you pay for the pre-warmed environments even when idle. (2) Lambda SnapStart (Java) — takes a snapshot of the initialized execution environment and restores it on invocation, reducing cold starts by up to 90%. (3) Keep deployment packages small — smaller packages initialize faster. Move dependencies to Layers. (4) Avoid VPC unless necessary — VPC Lambda cold starts take longer due to ENI creation. (5) Use scheduled EventBridge rule to ping the function every 5 minutes, keeping it warm. (6) Choose lighter runtimes — Python and Node.js have faster cold starts than Java and .NET. Trade-off: Provisioned Concurrency is the most reliable solution but increases cost. For most workloads, occasional cold starts are acceptable.
